Anchorage and laps

EN 1992-1-1, 8.4 and 8.7, for the bars of the section on the Section page. Bond conditions and cd come from where the bars are drawn. The design basis (National Annex) is set under Materials; the defaults are the recommended values.

–

Shear and edges

EN 1992-1-1, 6.2 for shear, 9.2.2 and 9.3.2 for links, 9.3.1.4 for free edges, for the section on the Section page. bw, d, the tension bars and the link legs come from the drawing. The defaults are the recommended values; use your National Annex.

Design basis and details

The materials and the design basis (National Annex) of the SOFiSTiK model, the bar lists, and the details of each group. These settings belong to the model; the simple sketch program keeps its own. The defaults are the recommended values.

Bar schedule

Check

What has to be cleared before the reinforcement is signed: the bars against what is required (as typed on step 2, and element by element against SOFiSTiK's results when they are open), the minimum reinforcement and the largest spacing (EN 1992-1-1, with the values of the design basis set on step 3), anchorage where elements meet, bars outside the concrete, and covers that do not fit. Fix an item, or accept it with a reason; accepted items are saved with the project and listed apart.

Project

Kept with the project (saved, in the link, undone with Ctrl+Z). What is filled in is printed at the top of the check, the calculation tables, the bar schedules and the exports. The drawing gets a title block when Title block on the drawing is ticked under Drawing.

New project

Starts afresh with the defaults. The sections, their anchorage settings and the drawing marks are cleared. Use Save project first to keep what you have; Ctrl+Z also brings it back until the page is closed.

Starts afresh with the defaults. The required reinforcement, zones, joins, anchorage settings, the sections cut from the model, the drawing marks and the pictures under the plans are cleared. Use Save project first to keep what you have; Ctrl+Z also brings it back until the page is closed.

Every version of this program opened in this browser shares the same storage, so a new version starts with what an older one left behind. Starting afresh shows what this version does by itself. The other program (simple sketch or SOFiSTiK model) keeps its own work and is not touched.

Guide

Everything is in millimetres, with the origin at the bottom left. The preview updates as you type; scroll to zoom and drag to pan. The grid shows 1 cm and 5 cm on paper at the drawing scale.

Simple sketch

This program draws cross-sections freely. The numbered steps at the top are its pages: draw the section and its bars (1 Section), work out its anchorage and laps (2 Anchorage and laps), check its shear and detail its free edges (3 Shear and edges), and see its bars along the member in 3D with a bar schedule (4 3D and schedule).

Reinforcing a SOFiSTiK model is a program of its own: the label at the top left goes back to the start page, where it can be chosen. The two keep their work apart.

SOFiSTiK model

This program reinforces a SOFiSTiK model. Model and design the structure in SOFiSTiK first; then the numbered steps at the top are its pages: read the model (1 Model); give the required reinforcement from SOFiSTiK's design, per group and element, and sketch zones that need more on a plan of each element (2 Required reinforcement); check the anchorage and laps and set the details (3 Anchorage and details)set the design basis and the details (3 Design basis and details); look at the bars in 3D, fine-tune them and export them to Tekla to finish the small things there (4 3D model and export).

A section checked through the 3D model, or cut on step 1 (Draw its bars in the editor), opens as a cross-section with all its checks; the step A Section appears for it next to the four steps.

One place for each thing. The steps at the top are the only way between the pages. Under them, every step has a ribbon with its options in tabs (File, Units and direction, View, Cuts on step 1; Zones, Picture, View on step 2; Export on step 3; View, Model, Export on step 4; Notes where there are any); click the open tab to fold the ribbon away. Step 2 takes what SOFiSTiK's design asks for: cm²/m for areas and their zones, cm² and cm²/m for beams and columns. Step 4 chooses the bars for it, and is the only place where Ø, spacing and the number of bars are set; a blank one is chosen and shown greyed.

Beams and columns. Structural lines with a cross-section (SNO) are read with their AQUA section (SREC, SCIT, or SECT with VERT corners) and material; only concrete is reinforced (steel sections are left out with a note). They show on the plan and in 3D as their section along the line, with labels, and get longitudinal bars (bottom, top and sides, or around a round section) and closed links. Their bars run on by lbd into the element they stand on or end in, bent along its far face where the straight length does not fit (a column into a footing or a slab), and stop at the cover where there is no concrete to go into. They are in the schedule, on step 3 and in the Tekla export (as parts with the section's outline).

Free cross-sections are a program of their own (simple sketch): the label at the top left goes back to the start page, where it can be chosen. The two keep their work apart.

Working with the app

  • Undo and redo (top bar, Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y) cover every change: values in the forms, the bar list, the drawing and the anchorage page. Typing in one box counts as one step.
  • Project… (top bar) holds the project name and number, the part or element, who designed and checked it, the revision, the date (Today fills it in) and a note. It is kept with the project: saved, in the link, and undone with Ctrl+Z; New… clears it. What is filled in is printed as the first line of the check (the dialog and the copied text), of the anchorage and laps tables (copy and print), of the bar schedules when copied, and of the OBJ export, and it goes into the Tekla file as project. Saved project files start with the project number. For a section drawing, Title block on the drawing (Drawing, Paper and text) adds a small table with the project, part, revision and date, designed and checked, and the scale at the bottom right of the drawing, in the SVG, PDF, DXF and PNG.
  • Forms are grouped; click a group heading to fold it, and the app remembers which groups you keep open. Greyed-out text in a box is what a blank box means; hover a ? for an explanation. In number boxes ↑ and ↓ step the value (Shift ×10, Alt ×0.1); a value that is not a number turns red.
  • The panel on the left: drag its right edge to make it wider or narrower (double-click for the default), or hide it with « to give the drawing the whole width (» brings it back).
  • The status bar shows the bars and areas on one line; Top / bottom, anchorage opens the rest. Warnings are always shown.

Finding coordinates

  • Rulers along the bottom and left edge of the drawing give the coordinates in mm, the red arrows mark the origin (0, 0), and the box at the bottom left shows x and y under the mouse. Near a corner or a bar it shows that point's coordinates and names it (on a custom section: outline point 3 is the third line of the Outline box). The ruler button next to Fit switches all of this off.
  • # numbers the outline points as they appear in the Outline box, the openings O1, O2 … and the links L1, L2 … (custom sections).
  • Pick a point: the target button next to an x, y pair in a reinforcement item sets both by clicking on the drawing. Draw on the drawing above a list of points replaces the list with points you click. Points snap to corners, bars and edges, and elsewhere to the grid (the step follows the zoom). Shift keeps a line horizontal or vertical, Alt places a point freely, right-click or Backspace takes the last point back, Enter or a double-click finishes, Esc cancels.

Editing shapes on the drawing (custom sections, Edit tool)

  • Outline and openings: with the Geometry tab open, the corners are blue squares. Drag one to move it; drag the + in the middle of an edge to add a corner there; right-click a corner to delete it. Openings can be moved by their centre, rectangles resized by a corner, circles by the diamond on the edge. The Outline and Openings boxes follow, and comments, arcs and break lines on the other lines are kept. Clicking the concrete with Edit opens the Geometry tab.
  • Draw a new outline and Add a rectangular opening on the Geometry tab work by clicking on the drawing.
  • Reinforcement items: select an item in the list (or click its bars) and drag its blue points: the ends of a row, the points of a line bar or link polygon, the corners of a link rectangle, the centre and radius of a circle pattern (the radius point also sets the start angle), a layer (sideways only, which sets its offset), the line of a dimension and a text. The crosshair point moves the whole item. Items that follow the section, such as a link along the outline, have no points to drag.
  • Dragging snaps to corners, bars and the grid; Alt drags freely, Shift keeps it straight, Esc puts it back. Every change can be undone.

Standard sections

Pick a type and fill in the fields. Layer tables take one row per layer, from the outer face inwards; gap is the clear distance to the layer before it (blank = the minimum spacing). Edit as custom copies the section, reinforcement included, into the custom editor as a starting point.

Custom sections

  • One custom section is kept while you work on standard sections. Coming back from a different standard section, a note offers to keep it, start blank or copy that standard section instead. New section or shape… on the Geometry tab starts a new section from a template, copies any standard section, or changes only the shape and keeps the bars. Undo brings the previous section back.
  • Outline: one vertex per line, x, y. Add an angle for an arc to the next vertex (0, 300, 180 is a half circle), and brk to draw the next edge as a break line. Pasting from Excel works.
  • Openings: rect x y w h, circle cx cy D or poly x1 y1 x2 y2 ….
  • Quick reinforcement (top of the Reinforcement tab) fills the list for the outline in one go, at the cover and with the minimum spacing between layers: beam or column (link, bottom, top and side bars), walls, slabs and frames (transverse and longitudinal bars on every straight face, for any shape such as U-frames, box girders or stairs; short end faces can be left out), bars around the outline (columns, piles, round sections) or hollow or box section (links and bars on the outer faces and around the openings). The items it makes are ordinary items you can change, and Undo takes them back.
  • Face layer: bars along chosen faces in any direction, at cover or inside a link: the inner face of a wall, an inclined slab, a web. Give the faces by the number of their first point (# on the drawing shows them; 2-4 for several, all for every straight face, O1 for the faces of an opening), or use Pick a face and Add a face on the drawing. Layers on the same face stack inwards at the minimum spacing, and the ends stop at the cover of the next face, so corners meet cleanly.
  • Layer: bars parallel to a face. Bottom and top give horizontal layers, left and right vertical ones. With a blank offset, layers from the same face stack inwards at the minimum spacing.
  • Perimeter: bars around the outline or the openings, with a bar in every corner and the bars between spread evenly face by face. Under More control: only around one opening, a different Ø for the corner bars, 2 or 3 rings inwards at the minimum spacing (or a gap you give), an extra distance inwards, and faces whose bars are left out (by the numbers # shows). The quickest way to add one is the Rebar tool's Bars around: click inside the section, or inside an opening; it goes inside the link around it if there is one.
  • Bar set: bars one by one, each line x, y with an optional own Ø. With Edit, drag a bar, right-click one to delete it, drag a + to add one between two bars, or click a bar to change its position or Ø in the panel (Previous and Next step through them). Add bars on the drawing adds bars where you click. Make each bar editable on a perimeter, layer, face layer, row or circle pattern turns its bars into a bar set, keeping its label; the bars then no longer follow changes to the outline.
  • Link: follows the outline, the part inside a rectangle or polygon, or runs around an opening. Links are numbered in list order; bars with Inside link no. stay inside that link.
  • List and drawing: the item selected in the list is shown in blue on the drawing, and hovering an item lights up its bars. With Edit, clicking a bar on the drawing opens its item; with Remove, it deletes the item.
  • Row, circle pattern, single bar, line bar, dimension, text: free placement.

Measuring and editing the drawing

  • Measure: click two points, then move the mouse to place the dimension line and click again. Points snap to corners, edges, bar centres, bar faces and link faces; hold Alt to place a point freely. Choose Along the two points for sloping measurements. Esc or right-click cancels.
  • Add text: click where the text should go and type it.
  • Edit text: click any label, title or dimension to change what it says. For a dimension, an empty text brings back the measured value.
  • Draw: Pencil draws thin freehand lines, Marker colours areas with a broad see-through stroke, Arrow and Circle are dragged out, and Tag places numbered markers (1, 2, 3 …) you can refer to in the text. Pick a colour and a width in the bar under the tools.
  • Move: drag any label, title, text, dimension, drawing or section view to a new place. Dimensions move sideways only, so they keep measuring the same points. Dragging the background pans.
  • Edit: besides the words, the formatting bar sets font, size, bold, italic, underline and colour, as in a word processor. Font on the Drawing tab changes the default for all text.
  • Rebar: Row of bars places bars (cut by the section) along a line you click from start to end, by spacing or number. Bar along a line draws a bar lying in the section plane; click its points and double-click or press Enter to finish. Points also snap to the line where a bar of the chosen Ø sits at cover (inside the links), and to its corners, so drawn bars keep the cover. Shift keeps a segment horizontal or vertical. On a custom section the bars go into the reinforcement list, where you can fine-tune them.
  • Changing a bar you drew: with Edit, click the bar. A box opens with its Ø, spacing or number and its coordinates; drag the blue points on the drawing to move the ends or corners, or drag the bar itself to move all of it, and the coordinates follow (in the reinforcement list as well). Remove deletes it. Move never picks up bars, so dragging a label or text next to a bar cannot shift the bar. This works for rows, single bars and line bars from the reinforcement list too.
  • Cut: click two points across the section. A section along the member (A–A, B–B …) appears beside the drawing, showing the concrete with break lines, longitudinal bars as lines, links at their spacing and in-plane bars as dots. Drag the cut line to move the cut, or drag the view to place it.
  • Remove: click a label, title, dimension or drawing to take it off the drawing. Restore brings back the predefined ones; Undo reverses the last change.
  • Scroll to zoom in any mode; drag with the middle mouse button (or hold Space) to pan while measuring. Shortcuts: H move, M measure, T text, E edit, D draw, B rebar, C cut, R remove, F fit the drawing, Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+Y redo.
  • Measurements belong to the section they were drawn on and appear in every export. They stay where you put them, so check them after changing the geometry.

SOFiSTiK models

Step 1 of the SOFiSTiK model workflow reads the model. From there you reinforce its elements (step 2), or cut sections out of it for the cross-section workflow.

  • .dat files: the Teddy input with the structural points, lines and areas (SPT, SLN with SLNB, SAR with SARB) and SYST for the direction of gravity. Open the main file together with the files it includes (pick several at once, or add them afterwards); #include Geometry.dat is then read from the file you opened, and the page lists any included file that is missing. Comments, ;, LET#/STO# variables (also from TEMPLATE blocks), LOOP and IF, #define with $(…) and #define blocks, and units such as 300[mm] are understood. Records of other programs (AQUA, SOFILOAD, ASE …) are skipped, and so are items the page does not need. A model built in SOFiPLUS can be written to a .dat with Export to DAT or EXPO.
  • SAF files (.xlsx): SOFiSTiK's SAF export writes the model as it is in the database, so it works whatever way the input was written. The 2D members (StructuralSurfaceMember with their nodes, thickness and system plane, and their openings) are read; their layers become the groups. This is the safest route for models with geometry the .dat reader cannot follow, for example points given relative to an axis.
  • Beams (lines with a cross-section) are not part of the cuts.
  • Units: coordinates are taken in m and the thickness T is guessed from its values (m or mm), unless the file gives a unit. Check the size shown under the file name, and change them under Units and direction if needed. Up is taken from GDIR.
  • The views: Plan shows the areas from above, coloured by group; 3D can be turned by dragging. Scroll to zoom, drag to pan. Click an area to see its number, group, thickness and side, to leave it out of the cuts, or to put its thickness on the other side of its surface (QREF ABOV or BELO). Groups can be left out of all cuts.
  • Cuts: Draw a cut on the plan and click two points across the structure (they snap to the corners of the areas; Shift keeps the line square to x or y). The cut is vertical and only reaches between the two points; the arrows show the direction it is seen in, and Reverse turns it round. Drag its ends or the line to move it, or type the coordinates. Add a level cut makes a horizontal cut, for walls and columns.
  • The section: every area the cut passes through gives a strip of its thickness, with ends that follow the area's edges; curved and warped areas are cut as surfaces. Areas modelled at their mid-surfaces leave notches where they meet; Close the corners where areas meet fills them. The strips are joined into one outline, and enclosed spaces, such as the cell of a box girder, become openings. If the cut has separate parts, choose the one to use (or click it in the picture).
  • Bars: Draw its bars in the editor opens the section in the custom editor with its 0, 0 at its lowest left corner, and sets a drawing scale to suit its size. Each section keeps its own bars, texts and anchorage settings: opening another section stores the one you were working on. Moving a cut updates its section, bars included, until you change the outline in the editor yourself.
  • The model is kept in this browser and in Save project files. A Copy link carries the sections but not the model. The browser keeps the large items (the model files, SOFiSTiK's results and the pictures under the plans) in its own database, which holds far more than the usual 5 MB; a copy that an older version left behind is moved there when this version starts. A saved project also carries the results that are open, so the check gives the same answer when the project is opened on another PC. A project saved before has no results: open them again.

SOFiSTiK's design results (step 2)

  • Have SOFiSTiK write them: Get rebar_export.dat on step 2 (it is also in the SOFiSTiK model folder), put it next to your .dat and add the line #INCLUDE rebar_export.dat at the end of the .dat, after the design (BEMESS). Every calculation then ends with a +PROG TEMPLATE block that reads the database (nodes, elements, groups, BEMESS's PARA/DIRE/GEOM and the required reinforcement of every design case) and writes <project>.rebar.txt next to the .cdb, in about 20 s. Nothing else is needed: no Python, no Grasshopper; the database is only read.
  • Or export them: after the design of the shells in SOFiSTiK, drop the .cdb on Export results.cmd (in the SOFiSTiK model folder), or double-click it and pick the file. It writes <model>.results.json next to the .cdb: the required reinforcement of every element, the largest of the design cases. It runs on your PC with Rhino 8's Python (or any Python 3.9+) and SOFiSTiK's own CDB interface; the .cdb is read from a copy and nothing is sent anywhere.
  • Open them on step 2 (Results > Open results, the .rebar.txt or the .results.json, or drop the file on step 1 with the .dat files). Each element gets what it needs everywhere (the mesh that needs the least steel with its zones), and zones R<SAR>.n where it needs more. Faces and directions are matched by their vectors, and the results must lie on the model's areas, or that area is left out with a note.
  • After a new calculation open the new file: empty cells and those still holding the results' last value follow the results; a value you typed is yours and is kept and checked. Zones from the results are made again, unless you moved or changed them. The Results section lists what changed, what was kept, and what falls short; Ctrl+Z undoes it all.
  • BEMESS's basic reinforcement: when the .dat holds the BEMESS input (+PROG BEMESS with GEOM, DIRE and PARA, in table form too, with sto# variables), each group on step 2 gets its PARA values: ASU, ASU2, ASL, ASL2 in cm²/m with the diameters DU, DU2, DL, DL2 (the first PARA without NOG is the default for all groups). DIRE UPP / LOW tells which direction the main bars run (DIRE 90: along local y), for the groups and for which result layer is which. With it, every element follows its group, and zones are made only where the results need more than the basic bars give. A value you type in a group is kept; Take from BEMESS again overwrites them. Covers stay as set; the groups' note lists where BEMESS's GEOM puts the layers, to compare. When the .dat has no BEMESS input (parameters given in SSD's dialog), they come from the .cdb with the results file, which holds what BEMESS last ran with; when both are there and differ, the groups' note says so.
  • Directions: the results file gives the required reinforcement along each area's local x and y (Export results.cmd turns BEMESS's main / transverse layers by DIRE, read from the .cdb). Older results files are turned on the website by the .dat's DIRE.
  • On the plan: Required colours the elements by what they need (the face and direction chosen), Check shows in red where they need more than the bars give.

The check

  • The button next to the steps counts what has to be cleared before the reinforcement is signed (⚠ 7 to clear, or ✓ Check clear). It is counted again after every change. Click it for the list.
  • Required vs provided: what you typed on step 2 against the bars chosen for it, and, with SOFiSTiK's results open, every element of the mesh against the bars at its place (the element's mesh, or a zone's total).
  • Minimum reinforcement of each element's own bars, per face: slabs max(0.26 fctm/fyk, 0.0013)·b·d for the main bars and 20 % of that across (9.2.1.1, 9.3.1.1); walls 0.002 Ac vertical and max(25 % of that, 0.001 Ac) horizontal, half on each face (9.6.2, 9.6.3). Largest spacing: slabs 3h ≤ 400 and 3.5h ≤ 450 mm, walls 3h ≤ 400 vertical and 400 mm horizontal. These are the numbers in the recommended values; the ones in use come from the design basis set on step 3 (Design basis (National Annex) and National Annex values), and the check says which. Check them against the National Annex in force.
  • Design basis: the line at the top of the check (also in Copy as text, the step 3 tables and the Tekla file) names the National Annex setting, concrete class, fyk, γc, γs and αct, and lists any other value that differs from the recommended ones.
  • Anchorage where elements meet: bars that stop at the cover with no room to anchor or lap, bars that run only straight into the other element for less than lbd, and joints where one side stops for the other to lap but the other does not run on. Areas in one plane that are not joined cause most of these: the item says so.
  • Anchorage, laps and junctions are not designed in this version: the bars are the field reinforcement and end at the element edges or the cover; bar ends, laps and the details where elements meet are detailed by hand. The check lists this under what it does not cover.
  • Bars in the concrete: every bar is followed in 100 mm steps; points outside every element (the corners where elements meet count as concrete) are listed. Covers and fit: covers and layers thicker than the element, bars that do not fit in one row.
  • Results and model: the model files remember their own file time when you open them (also in a saved project). With results open, the check tells you when a model file is more than a minute newer than the results (calculate again and open the new results), and when the results come from another project name than the model. Nothing is said when a time is not known, as in projects saved before. Show goes to the results on step 2; the item can be accepted like the others.
  • Not covered by this check (the last part of the list, not counted in the button): shear and punching of slabs and walls, crack widths and deflections beyond the design cases in the results, the reinforcement of beams and columns (typed on step 2), fatigue, accidental situations and fire, and local regions such as concentrated loads, corbels, construction joints and openings beyond the trimmer bars. A clear check is therefore not a complete design check.
  • Show opens the element where it is fixed (step 2 for the results, with the check on its plan; step 4 for the bars). Accept… keeps an item as it is, with a reason; accepted items are saved with the project, listed apart, and can be reopened. Copy as text gives the whole list, open and accepted, for the calculation's notes.

Required reinforcement (A_s,req)

  • Standard sections: every bar table has an A_s,req column: cm² for rows given by a number of bars (beams, columns, piles), cm²/m for rows given by a spacing (slabs, walls).
  • Leave a box blank and it is chosen to cover As,req with the least steel: with a spacing given, the Ø; with a Ø given, the spacing (or the number of bars); with both blank, both. The chosen value is shown greyed in blue in the blank box, and the drawing, labels, anchorage, 3D and schedule use it.
  • With all given, the row is checked, and the status bar also says which Ø the given spacing (or number of bars) needs.
  • The Ø and spacings to choose from are set on the anchorage page (Bars chosen from a required area). Slabs and walls keep within the largest spacing of EN 1992-1-1, 9.3.1.1(3) (recommended: 3h ≤ 400 mm for the outer layer of a face, 3.5h ≤ 450 mm for the others) and 9.6 (recommended: 3h ≤ 400 mm); these numbers are set under National Annex values on the anchorage page; a typed spacing above it is warned about. In beams the number of bars is kept to what fits in one row, or a warning says to split them.
  • Custom sections: Layer and Face layer items have an A_s,req field (cm² with Distribution = count, cm²/m with a spacing); blank Ø, n or s are chosen in the same way.
  • The status bar lists every row with As,req: what was chosen or checked, and the area it gives.

Shear and edges

Step 3 checks the section on the Section page for shear to EN 1992-1-1, 6.2, with vertical links, and details free edges. The materials are those of the anchorage page.

  • From the drawing: the tension bars are the bars in the half of the depth next to the tension face (red in the picture), d runs from the compression face to their centroid, z = 0.9 d, bw is the least width over the lever arm, and the links count with the legs that cross the middle of the lever arm (circles). Shear acts and Tension face turn the check for walls, hogging or sideways shear.
  • Members: beams and columns always need links, at least ρw,min (9.2.2); slabs and walls are checked per metre and need shear reinforcement only where VEd > VRd,c (9.3.2), and the page then also gives the tension bars that would make VRd,c enough.
  • Results: VRd,c (6.2.a/b), and with the links drawn VRd,s and VRd,max at the strut angle that gives the most (6.8, 6.9). With VEd given, the page finds the flattest strut that VRd,max allows, the Asw/s needed, and proposes links from the lists on the left; a click sets the links of the section (Ctrl+Z undoes it). The detailing rules (ρw,min, sl,max, st,max, 6.5) are listed, and the whole calculation is written out.
  • Free edges (Slab and Wall): Free edge at closes an end of the strip with U-bars reaching 2h from the edge (Fig. 9.8), inside every layer of both faces, with bars along the edge in their bends (Ø, spacing and length default to the bars that end at the edge). The page checks the length, the spacing (9.3.1.1(3)), the bend (Table 8.1N) and the lap of the legs with the bars that end at the edge.
  • Bridge edge beam: the deck is checked for shear at the root of the cantilever, per metre, with its top bars in tension; and the edge beam for the anchorage of the deck's top bars bent down into it, its links (ρw,min, spacing) and its longitudinal bars (As,min).
  • The status bar shows the shear check once VEd is given.

3D and schedule (cross-sections)

Step 4 of the cross-section workflow builds the reinforcement of the section along the member, from what the section and the anchorage page describe.

  • Bars cut by the section run along the member in bars of the stock length, lapped by l0 and, with less than 100 % lapped in one section, staggered in sets by 1.3·l0, exactly as on Along the member. The two bars of a lap lie side by side, the second one towards the inside. At anchored member ends they stop at the cover and get the bar end chosen on the anchorage page: straight, a 90° bend or a loop, around a mandrel of 4Ø (Ø ≤ 16) or 7Ø (Table 8.1N), turned inwards.
  • Links and bars in the section plane are repeated at their spacing, links from s/2 and in-plane bars from s, as in a Cut view. A link without a spacing is drawn at 200 mm; an in-plane bar without one is drawn once, at mid-length. In-plane bars with a lap position (Calculation tab) are split there and lapped by l0.
  • Lengths from the model: when the section was cut from a SOFiSTiK model (and the model is open), the member length is the extent of the areas the cut passes through, measured square to the cut (vertical for a level cut), and the cut is shown where it lies in the member. The lap layout, the anchorage page and the schedule all use this length. Choose the length typed below under Member and lap layout to use your own. A level cut also makes the bars run vertically for the bond condition.
  • The bar schedule gives every different bar a mark, with its shape, number, centre-line length (bends included, rounded up to 10 mm) and weight; the same schedule is on the anchorage page. Hover a row to find its bars in the model, or hover a bar to see its mark and length.
  • Viewing: drag to turn, right-drag (or Shift+drag) to pan, scroll to zoom where the pointer is, double-click a point to turn around it; 3D, Section, Side and Top set the view and F fits it. Concrete, links, the bar types, the laps and the anchorage lengths can be switched on and off, and Show from … to … cuts the model to a part of its length. Colours go by position (top, bottom, sides) or by mark.
  • Exports: an OBJ file of what is shown (in mm, y up) for Rhino, Blender, Revit or a viewer, and the schedule for Excel.

Required reinforcement (SOFiSTiK model, step 2)

  • Groups: the reinforcement every element of a group needs, in cm²/m, upper and lower face, principal and cross direction (or the two directions of the global choice). Blank keeps the group's mesh as it is.
  • Element: pick one in the list (‹ › step through them); Values of its own gives it values that differ from its group. Everywhere is what it needs everywhere; the zones below are what it needs in total where more is needed. Under each value the bars chosen for it: from the bar lists of step 3 and within the largest spacing allowed, the least steel; in a zone the element's mesh counts and the bars added between it are shown with +; red where the bar lists cannot cover it.
  • Sketching zones on the plan of the element: Rectangle (R) drag across it, Polygon (P) click the corners (the first one again, a double-click or Enter finishes, Backspace takes one back), or Strip along … a line where it meets another element (1.5 m each side; the width is set in its row). Points snap to corners and lines, else to 50 mm; Alt places them freely. Select: click a zone, drag it to move it, Delete removes it; drag the background to pan, scroll to zoom, F fits. The dashed lines are where other elements meet it, and the red arrow is its local x-axis.
  • A picture under the plan: Picture… loads a screenshot of SOFiSTiK's reinforcement plot for the element; Line it up: click a point on the picture and then the same point of the element (a corner), twice, and the picture is scaled, turned and moved to fit. Trace the zones over it. Pictures are kept in this browser only, not in the project file.

Reinforcing the SOFiSTiK model

Step 4 of the SOFiSTiK workflow: the model in 3D with the bars of every element, its bar schedule and the export to Tekla. Here the bars are chosen for what step 2 asks: click a group in the panel, or an element in the view.

  • Faces and directions (ribbon, Model tab): as in SOFiSTiK, each area's faces are its upper face (against its local z-axis) and lower face, and the layers run in the principal direction (the local x-axis, or at the angle you give from it, towards local y) and the cross direction at right angles, and only these two are offered; by default the cross reinforcement is the outer layer and the principal reinforcement lies inside it. The local axes are read from the model: z along gravity, or against NX/NY/NZ (which give the upward side); x along DRX/DRY/DRZ, or else the global X-axis (Y for areas square to X) laid into the area, turned by DROT. Show draws them (x red, y green, z blue), and the panel says, for a picked element, where they point. The other choice names the faces top and bottom (walls +X / −X) and offers the global directions instead. Switching renames the layers to the other system by the way they run, so the bars stay where they are; layers that still carry names of the other system are renamed the same way when a step of the model is opened. Projects made before this choice keep the global one.
  • Elements: every element of the model, each with its own outline, openings and thickness, gets layers of bars on its two faces. Set them per group, or click an element and give it bars of its own: for each face the cover, and for each layer (its direction and the area step 2 asks for are shown) the Ø and spacing. A blank Ø or spacing is chosen to cover the requirement and shown greyed; a layer without a requirement needs both.
  • Joining areas: areas that are one piece of concrete but were modelled apart (a slab split into several areas, a wall split by storeys) can be joined into one element, and the bars then run through. Join touching areas in one plane does it for every group at once; or pick an element, choose Join with other areas… and click the areas (a joined one clicked again is taken out, Esc ends). Joined areas may differ in thickness: the bars step at 1:6 where they do, and follow a thickness that varies. Areas more than 25° out of plane, and curved areas, are not joined. Areas in one plane that touch but are not joined are lapped by l0 and listed in the notes.Areas in one plane that touch but are not joined are listed in the notes.
  • Where elements meet at an angle (a slab on a wall, a wall under a slab, two walls at a corner) the bars ending there run to the far face of the other element and turn along it, with a leg so that lbd is reached from its inner face (at least 10Ø past the bend, mandrel 4Ø or 7Ø); per group or element they can instead run straight to the far face, or stop at the cover. The panel lists for each element how much of its edge is free and what it meets.
  • Free edges can get U-bars (Ø and spacing; legs 2h, at least 300 mm, inside the outer layers; 9.3.1.4), and openings trimmer bars along each side on both faces, running lbd past the corners, and diagonal bars across the corners. Curved and warped areas get their bars along the surface, at the cover from both faces; their lengths are scheduled in 100 mm steps.
  • Runs longer than the stock length are lapped by l0, worked out for each layer's Ø, spacing, cover and bond (top bars of slabs thicker than 250 mm are in poor bond) with the settings of step 3, and staggered by ρ1. Levels from … to … shows one storey; the schedule lists every bar of the model by mark.
  • Each run of bars is one bar (no stock lengths, no laps); where an element meets another at 45° or more the bar runs straight to the far face of the other, otherwise it stops at the element's edge; at free edges it stops at the cover. Levels from … to … shows one storey; the schedule lists every bar of the model by mark, and its lengths exclude anchorage and laps.
  • Tekla Structures (Export): Tekla rebars (.json) writes every bar of the model (or only the isolated element) as its corner points with the bending radius, in the model's coordinates in mm (z up; a model with z down is turned 180° about x). The script (.py) reads it into the Tekla model that is open, through the Tekla Open API: run py -m pip install pythonnet once, then py tekla_rebars.py file.tekla.json. Bars of one shape at one spacing become a rebar group (stretch it, change the spacing, or ungroup it in Tekla), all others single rebars; the cover is set so the bar centre lines lie on the exported points; there are no hooks, and laps are two overlapping bars. Each bar needs a concrete part: by default the script attaches to the concrete part of the Tekla model where the bars are, and creates a panel from the area (outline, openings, thickness) where there is none; --concrete find, create or pick choose one way. Grade and size names depend on the Tekla environment: --grade and --size, or CONFIG at the top of the script. The script writes a log of what it created, and --remove with that log deletes it again before a new import.
  • Check a section: Check a section through it (an element) first asks where: a red plane, marked A–A with arrows the way it is seen, follows the pointer over the element; click where the cut goes (Enter takes the place shown, Esc cancels). It then opens a strip there as a cross-section (the step A Section) with the bars across the cut as dots at their spacing and depth, the others as lines, and all the checks of a cross-section; it is a copy, changes there do not go back to the model. Going back to step 4 frames the cut, which stays in the 3D view (View tab, Section A–A).
  • Isolate (View tab, or I): only the picked element, or every element of the picked group, is shown as it is, and the view frames it; the other elements are faded (glass-grey bars, faint concrete) or hidden (only faint concrete). Click another element, also a faded one, to isolate that one instead. I or Esc ends it.
  • Required areas come from step 2 and are shown with each layer. Leave Ø, s or both blank and they are chosen to cover it, with the least steel and then the wider spacing, from the diameters and spacings listed on step 3 and within the largest spacing of EN 1992-1-1; with both given they are checked.
  • Zones with more reinforcement are sketched on step 2 with what they need. Here, pick an element and click one of its zones on the small plan (or in the list) to choose its bars, and whether they are
    • in addition to the element's bars: a layer in the direction of one of the element's layers, at that spacing or a multiple of it, goes between the element's bars (Ø16/150 between Ø12/150 gives 75 mm centres), others go in a layer further in; they run lbd past the zone, or only to its edge; orthey run the effective depth d of the layer past the zone, or only to its edge; or
    • instead of the element's bars: on each face where the zone has layers, the element's bars stop at the zone edge and the zone's bars run l0 past it to lap with them.the element's bars stop at the zone edge and the zone's bars run the effective depth d past it.
    With a required area in a zone whose bars are in addition, the row is the total needed there: the element's bars of that direction count, and the zone adds only what they lack, between them (in every gap or every other gap); if they are enough, no bars are added. This is the usual base mesh plus top-up over supports or in fields. Zone bars that reach an edge meeting another element are anchored into it like the element's bars. Zones are shaded in their colour on the faces they have bars on, their bars are drawn in that colour, the schedule names them, and a section through the zone shows its bars beside the element's. Click a zone, or one of its bars, to edit it. Zones cannot be placed on curved areas.

Anchorage and details (SOFiSTiK model)Design basis and details (SOFiSTiK model)

Details per group: the cover of the upper and lower face, how bars end where an element meets another one (anchored with a bend, straight to the far face, or stopped at the cover), U-bars at free edges (legs of 2h) and the trimmer and diagonal bars at openings. Elements with values of their own keep them (step 4).

Step 3 of the SOFiSTiK workflow, with settings of its own: concrete class, fyk, partial factors, steel stress, share lapped in one section ρ1, bond (from position, or all good or all poor) and the bar length, and the bar lists. Copy the settings of the cross-sections takes them over in one go. Projects saved before this version keep the settings they were made with.

Design basis (National Annex), first field under Materials: EN 1992-1-1 recommended values (the default), Denmark, DK NA (only γc 1.45 and γs 1.20 differ; the other values are the recommended ones and must be checked against the National Annex in force) or own values. Choosing one writes its values into the fields below (one undo step); typing a value yourself switches to own values. The group National Annex values holds the factors for the minimum reinforcement and the largest spacing of slabs and walls (9.2.1.1, 9.3.1.1, 9.6.2, 9.6.3); the check, the bars chosen from a required area and the U-bar rules use them. The setting is printed at the top of the check, the tables (Copy tables, Print / PDF) and in the Tekla file.

  • Lap and anchorage lengths: one row for each Ø, spacing, cover and bond in the model, with cd, lbd, l0, the number of bars and laps, the bar ends bent into other elements, and where they are.
  • Anchorage and lap lengths are switched off in this version: the bars are the field reinforcement, so no lengths are tabulated here.
  • Elements and Zones: thickness, reinforcement, zones, edges, laps and weight of each elementthickness, reinforcement, zones, edges and weight of each element, and each zone with its area, bars and weight. Click a row to open it on step 2.
  • Required and provided reinforcement: every layer given a required area, with the bars chosen (or checked), what the element's bars give in a zone, the area provided and the percentage of the requirement.
  • Copy tables puts the lengths and the bar schedule on the clipboard for Excel; Print / PDF prints the tables, the schedule and the lengths for all diameters.Copy tables puts the bar schedule on the clipboard for Excel; Print / PDF prints the tables and the schedule. Bar lengths exclude anchorage and laps.

Saving and sharing

New… starts afresh with an empty project (optionally keeping the SOFiSTiK model file open); Ctrl+Z brings the old one back. The label next to the name shows which version of the app is running; all versions opened in one browser share its storage, so starting afresh is the way to see what a new version does by itself.

Your work is kept in this browser automatically. Save project downloads a .json file that Open… reads back. Copy link puts the whole section into a link you can send to a colleague.

Checks

Bar labels say whether a group is top or bottom reinforcement, and the lines under the title list the top, bottom and side reinforcement (both can be switched off on the Drawing tab). On a custom section each bar item has a Top or bottom field; auto takes the face of a layer, or otherwise the position: above or below the centroid, with the middle third of the height counted as sides.

Anchorage and lap lengths

Step 2 of the cross-section workflow is a page of its own for the section you are drawing (the SOFiSTiK model has its own, above). Each group of bars (same position, Ø and bond condition) gets lbd and l0 to EN 1992-1-1, 8.4 and 8.7. Set the concrete class, fyk, the steel stress, the share of bars lapped in one section and the partial factors on the left. Design basis (National Annex) under Materials sets the partial factors and the values under National Annex values (minimum reinforcement and largest spacing) in one go: EN 1992-1-1 recommended values (the default), Denmark (only γc 1.45 and γs 1.20 differ; check the other values against the National Annex in force) or own values. Typing a value yourself switches it to own values. The setting is printed at the top of the anchorage tables.

  • The table shows every bar group with lbd and l0, its bond as a coloured tag, and both lengths as bars to the same scale (light: anchorage, red: lap), so the long ones stand out. Show the factors adds cd and the products of the α factors. Click a row to work on that group.
  • Lap: the lap seen from the side, to scale along the bars: l0 in mm and in Ø, the bar ends (straight, bent or looped), and, where 8.7.4.1 asks for them (Ø ≥ 20 mm), the outer thirds where the transverse bars go, checked against the section's links. With less than 100 % lapped in one section the next set of bars is drawn with its lap staggered by 1.3 l0, the 0.3 l0 gap and the 0.65 l0 zone. In compression the bars within 4Ø outside the lap ends are marked. The buttons under the picture change the share lapped, the bond, tension or compression and the bar end in one click. How l0 is made shows each step from lb,rqd to l0 as a bar, so you see which factor matters; Rules for this lap lists the spacing, staggering and transverse-bar rules with this group's numbers.
  • Anchorage: the bar anchored past the point where it must carry its full force, with lbd, lb,rqd and lb,min on a ruler, how lbd is made, and the mandrel diameter for bends.
  • Calculation: every factor written out with the numbers put in, the section with the group's bars highlighted, and all the inputs for one group.
  • All diameters: lbd and l0 for Ø6 to Ø40 in good and poor bond with the page settings, ready to copy into a drawing note.
  • For one group you can set every parameter of Table 8.2: the bond condition, tension or compression, the steel stress; α₁ and α₂ from the bar end (straight, bent or hooked, looped) and your own a, c₁ and c (Fig. 8.3; blank uses what the drawing measures); α₃ from K (Fig. 8.4), the transverse bars (Ø, spacing, legs, or a link of the section with one click) and beam or slab; α₄ for a welded transverse bar; α₅ from the transverse pressure p; and α₆ from ρ₁. α₂·α₃·α₅ is kept at 0.7 or more, and α₃ for laps uses ΣAst,min = As·σsd/fyd. Changed rows are marked ✎; Use the page values for this group undoes it.
  • Along the member: the member seen from the side, one lane per group of bars cut by the section (hover a bar or a lap to see where it runs). The member length, bar length and ends can be changed right there, and the bar schedule of the 3D model lists every bar with its mark, centre-line length, number and weight. When the section was cut from a SOFiSTiK model, the member length is taken from the model (see 3D model below). Bars of the stock length are laid from the left end and lapped by l₀; with ρ₁ below 100 % they are split into sets with laps staggered by 1.3·l₀ (0.3·l₀ clear, Fig. 8.7). The member length, bar length and ends are set on the left, the bar length also per group. Bars lying in the section plane get a lap position along the bar, and the lap is drawn on the group's section picture.
  • Bond condition comes from where each bar sits, as the section is drawn (cast from the top): good for h ≤ 250 mm, within 250 mm of the bottom, or more than 300 mm below the top when h > 600 mm; poor otherwise. Bars running vertically (columns, piles, plan sections of walls) and in-plane bars at 45° or more are good. Edges drawn as break lines count as continuing concrete.
  • α₂ uses cd = min(a/2, c) measured on the drawing (clear distance to the nearest bar, cover to the nearest real face); the smallest cd of a group governs. α₃, α₄ and α₅ are 1, which is on the safe side.
  • Print / PDF prints every group with its workings; Copy table copies the table for Excel. A summary table can also go on the section drawing (ticked on the page).
  • The results are indicative: the steel stress is the value you give, not taken from an analysis.

The status bar shows As, Ac and ρ, with As for each of top, bottom and sides (cm² for counted bars, cm²/m for bars given by spacing), and warns about overlapping bars and clear spacing below max(Ø, dg + 5 mm, 20 mm). It is a sketching aid, not a design check.
